messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened on a warm September night, just after her nineteenth birthday. Leila had been walking home from a friend’s apartment when a man emerged from the alley beside the shuttered laundromat. She remembered the smell of alcohol on his breath, thick and sour, before he grabbed her wrist and pulled her into the darkness. He shouted in Arabic—words she did not understand but whose cadence she would never forget—and then the motorcycle roared past, its engine drowning out her scream. She had not thought she could stop it. Somebody else would have, she later told herself, somebody braver or faster. She had frozen, and that failure became the story she told herself about who she now was.

In the weeks that followed, Leila found she could not control when the memory returned. A passing motorcycle on the street outside her apartment would bring it back without warning—the full sensory flood: the alcohol smell, the shouting, the vibration of the engine through her bones. She would hear the man’s voice in her head, the exact pitch and rhythm, as though he were still there. She began to avoid going out after dark, and she stopped looking at her own body in the mirror, because seeing the faint bruise that had long since faded made her feel the grip on her wrist again. She also avoided the date—September 14th—as though the calendar itself was a trap.

Her husband, Omar, worked the evening shift at a warehouse, and Leila spent her nights alone in their small apartment. She listened constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering: the creak of the hallway floorboards, the jingle of keys, the click of the lock. Every noise seemed intentional. She would get up three or four times to check the chain, and when she finally lay back down, the memory would surge again—the alley, the shouting, the smell—and she would be certain that she was no longer capable of the simple things that had once defined her: walking home, trusting a quiet street, feeling safe in her own skin. The more she checked, the more the memories intruded, and the more she believed that someone else would have handled it better, that she had been weak.

She began to look behind her constantly, even in daylight, even inside the grocery store. She told herself it was caution, but the checking fed something darker: each time she saw nothing, she felt relief, but the relief never lasted, and the next glance confirmed that danger was always possible. The world had become a place where a man could appear from nowhere, and her beliefs about how things worked—that people were basically good, that bad things happened to other people—had been destroyed. She started to hear the shouting in her head more often, triggered by nothing she could name, and then she would smell the alcohol again, and the cycle would tighten.

By the time winter came, Leila had not left the apartment after four in the afternoon for three months. She had stopped answering calls from her mother, who did not understand why her daughter had become so distant. Omar had started sleeping on the couch because she would wake him at 2 a.m. to check the door. She knew this was not normal, but she also knew that if she stopped listening, stopped checking, stopped avoiding, something terrible would happen. It was Omar who finally found a clinic number and handed it to her. She took it because she was exhausted, but what frightened her most was the thought that even therapy could not undo what she had become.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about weakness).
No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences triggers (e.g., makes cues more salient).
No paragraph conveys that avoidance or checking (maladaptive strategies) causally influences sense of threat.
